newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan denies offering US$500 mln aid to Liberia.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan denies offering US$500 mln aid to Liberia.

text.p: Taiwan on Thursday said it was willing to offer aid to war-torn Liberia, but not the US$500 million that a military strongman in the West African country told news media.
"It is quite unlikely for us to offer Liberia such a huge amount of aid," Foreign Minister John Chang said.
Chang, speaking on state radio, said the ministry simply did not have that kind of money to offer Liberia.

Strongman Charles Taylor was quoted by Taiwan's state-run Central News Agency and other media as saying Taipei had offered US$500 million to help the country rebuild itself after a seven-year civil war.
The foreign ministry said it was willing to offer aid in a bid to cement ties with Liberia, whose government wants relations with Taiwan and its arch rival, China.
China, which has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, is eager to win Liberia over completely to its side.
Beijing refuses to recognise countries that recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China, but has tolerated Liberia's dual recognition.

Monrovia signed a pact forging official ties with Taiwan in 1989 shortly before the country entered a civil war. A faction headed by Liberian warlord Amos Sawyer established diplomatic relations with Beijing in 1993.

Major Taiwan news media on Monday received a faxed statement from Ruth Perry, chairwoman of the State Council of Liberia National Transitional Government, asserting that Monrovia maintained diplomatic ties only with China, not Taiwan.
Taiwan's foreign ministry rejected Perry's position.
The ministry said Taiwan's Liberian ties were firm and unaffected by the 1993 Beijing move.
Taipei has diplomatic relations with just 30 states, mostly underdeveloped countries in Africa and Latin America that rely heavily on the island's generous aid.
